::: {.lead-box}
The methods presented in the lecture — surrogate models, Bayesian optimisation, anomaly
detection, classification, reinforcement learning — are not specific to accelerators. This page
maps them onto problems of **reactor physics, plant operation, radiation protection, dosimetry
and the fuel cycle**, and proposes three notebooks built on nuclear-energy problems.
:::

## A common pattern
In most of these applications **labelled real data are rare** (accidents, faults and exotic
sources do not happen on demand). The training data come from **simulation codes** — Serpent,
OpenMC, MCNP, Geant4, plant simulators — and the ML model learns to invert or accelerate them.
The quality of the simulation, and the gap between simulation and reality, then decide how
well the model works in the field. All three notebooks below make this point explicitly.
:::

## Three hands-on case studies

All three run on Google Colab with **nothing to install** (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn,
matplotlib) and use small, transparent physics simulators written in the notebook itself.

### 4 · Radionuclide identification in gamma spectra {#gamma}

NaI(Tl) spectra of activation and fission products (Co-60, Co-58, Mn-54, Eu-152, Cs-137,
Cs-134, I-131…) over natural background. Classical region-of-interest analysis vs. a
**neural network** vs. a physics-based **full-spectrum fit**; counting statistics; **gain drift**
and data augmentation; what happens with a nuclide outside the library.

[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hayg25/ML4Accelerators/blob/main/notebooks/04_gamma_spectroscopy.ipynb)
&nbsp; solution: [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hayg25/ML4Accelerators/blob/main/notebooks/solutions/04_gamma_spectroscopy.ipynb)

### 5 · A surrogate model of a reactor-physics code {#reactor}

A toy PWR pin-cell code (six-factor formula, Doppler, boron, moderator density) with Monte
Carlo-like noise plays the role of an expensive transport code. Latin-hypercube design of 40
runs, **Gaussian-process surrogate** with uncertainty, critical boron search, reactivity
coefficients, **uncertainty propagation** with 10⁵ samples, GP vs. neural network with few
data, active learning.

[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hayg25/ML4Accelerators/blob/main/notebooks/05_reactor_surrogate.ipynb)
&nbsp; solution: [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hayg25/ML4Accelerators/blob/main/notebooks/solutions/05_reactor_surrogate.ipynb)

### 6 · Neutron/gamma pulse-shape discrimination {#psd}

Photoelectron-level simulation of liquid-scintillator pulses. Optimised charge comparison vs. a
**neural network** on raw waveforms; figure of merit; performance versus energy; **pile-up**;
neutron efficiency at a fixed gamma-rejection level.

[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hayg25/ML4Accelerators/blob/main/notebooks/06_neutron_gamma_psd.ipynb)
&nbsp; solution: [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hayg25/ML4Accelerators/blob/main/notebooks/solutions/06_neutron_gamma_psd.ipynb)

## What the three notebooks have in common

The notebooks were designed to give an **honest** picture, not a sales pitch:

- **ML is not automatically better.** A well-optimised physics-based method (full-spectrum fit,
  tail-to-total ratio) is as good as a neural network when the physics model is exact and the
  signal clean. Always compare with the *best* classical method.
- **ML pays off when conditions vary or are hard to model**: detector drift, pile-up,
  background changes — provided the training data contain them.
- **With few, expensive data, prefer Gaussian processes** over neural networks: they need
  tens of runs instead of thousands, and give error bars.
- **A model knows only its training domain**: unknown nuclides, extrapolation, new operating
  conditions require explicit checks.

## Using the notebooks for group work

Each notebook takes 45–60 min for a group of 3–4 people. Suggested discussion questions for
the final presentation:

1. In your own research, which quantity is expensive to compute or to measure, and what would a
   surrogate or a classifier need as training data?
2. Where would the training data come from (which code, which measurements), and how would you
   check that the model still works on the real system?
3. What would be the consequence of a wrong prediction, and how would you keep a human — or a
   physics-based check — in the loop?
